analysis.one_liner: Blocks EPA from finalizing any energy rule costing over $1 billion if the Energy Department finds economic harm.
analysis.headline: The House passed it 232-181 on August 1, 2013, but the Senate never voted, and it died when the 113th Congress ended in January 2015.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require the EPA, before finalizing any energy-related rule estimated to cost more than $1 billion, to report its costs, benefits, energy-price impacts, and job effects to Congress. It would then require the Energy Department to do its own analysis of whether the rule raises energy prices or hurts energy supply, and it would flatly bar the EPA from finalizing the rule if the Energy Department determines it will significantly harm the economy. A House-added section also bans the EPA from using the 'social cost of carbon' — the government's dollar estimate of climate damage — in any such rule's cost-benefit analysis unless Congress passes a law authorizing it. [S2] [S4] [S5]
analysis.who_benefits: Energy producers, above all coal mines and coal-fired power plants, that were facing expensive EPA limits on pollution and carbon emissions. The bill gives them a procedural shield: any major EPA energy rule could be vetoed by the Energy Department, and the climate-cost side of the government's accounting would be switched off. [S2] [S5]

how_it_helps.text: For any EPA energy rule estimated to cost over $1 billion, the bill requires reports on total costs, energy-price increases, and job effects, plus an independent Energy Department analysis of impacts on prices, fuel diversity, and electric reliability. [S2] [S5]

The bill prohibits the EPA from finalizing any such rule if the Secretary of Energy determines it will cause significant adverse effects to the economy, giving one cabinet department veto power over the EPA's biggest energy rules. [S2] [S5]

The version the House passed also bans use of the social cost of carbon in cost-benefit analysis for those rules unless a federal law authorizes it, removing the dollar value of avoided climate damage from the government's math. [S4] [S5]

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary people bear the health and climate costs of EPA rules the bill could block, including rules that reduce pollution even when their benefits outweigh their costs. Energy consumers would still face the pollution those rules were written to prevent; the bill reports rule benefits but does not let them stop a ban. [S2] [S5]
analysis.who_pays_short: Households exposed to pollution and climate damage

drawbacks.text: The bill hands the Energy Department — an agency charged with promoting energy production — veto power over any EPA energy rule costing over $1 billion, so a rule with large health and climate benefits could be blocked whenever the Secretary finds economic harm. [S5]

Banning the social cost of carbon means the government's cost-benefit math for major energy rules would count compliance costs but not the damages from carbon pollution, tilting every analysis against regulation until Congress acts. [S5]

Supporters' honest case is that compliance costs for energy rules flow to households and businesses through utility bills and that the social cost of carbon estimate had never been approved by Congress; the bill's reporting requirements respond to that. But the remedy it chose was not better analysis — it was the power to block rules outright. [S2] [S4]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The transparency and reporting pieces are uncontroversial, but the bill's core is a near-blanket veto over the EPA's largest energy rules plus removal of climate damages from the government's accounting. That design makes it easier to block rules whose benefits to public health and the climate exceed their costs, and the burden of blocked pollution falls on ordinary people rather than on the industries regulated.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it on a nearly party-line vote, but after the Senate referred it to its environment committee in September 2013, that committee never acted, and the bill died when the Congress ended. [S7]

narrative.text: The House Energy and Commerce Committee ordered the bill reported by a vote of 25-18 on July 17, 2013, and reported it amended on July 22. [S7]

Before final passage, Rep. Lois Capps moved to send the bill back to committee with instructions to add an exemption for any rules that would reduce cancer, premature death, or asthma attacks in children and seniors; it failed 188-221, with all voting Republicans opposed and all voting Democrats in favor. [S7] [S8]
The House passed the bill 232-181 on August 1, 2013: 223 of 233 voting Republicans in favor, 9 of 200 voting Democrats in favor. [S9]

The Senate received the bill on September 9, 2013, and referred it to the Committee on Environment and Public Works, which took no further action before the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015. [S7]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never became law, the EPA kept its authority to finalize major energy and climate rules, and the energy producers the bill was written to shield never got that protection. People who would breathe the air and bear the climate effects of blocked rules came out ahead; the industries facing those rules did not.

for.name: Bill Cassidy
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and managed it on the House floor.

for.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
for.what_they_did: Marked up the bill, ordered it reported 25-18, and reported it amended on July 22, 2013.

against.name: Senate Environment and Public Works Committee
against.role: Committee of referral in the Senate
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on September 9, 2013, and never took it up, keeping it from any Senate vote.

against.name: Lois Capps
against.what_they_did: Moved to recommit the bill with instructions to exempt rules that reduce cancer, premature death, and asthma attacks in children and seniors; the motion failed 188-221.

against.name: President Obama
against.what_they_did: The administration publicly opposed the bill, which faced no chance of being signed in its House-passed form.

sides.party_line_note: Final passage split almost entirely by party: 223 of 233 voting Republicans yes versus 9 of 200 voting Democrats; the Capps motion to recommit split 188-221 with every voting Republican opposed and every voting Democrat in favor. [S8] [S9]

industries.industry: Coal mining and coal-fired power plants
industries.note: The bill would shield them from EPA rules on energy production costing over $1 billion whenever the Energy Department finds economic harm, and would strip carbon's climate damages from the analysis. Their gain comes at the cost of pollution and climate exposure for the public. [S2] [S5]

As energy producers, they would benefit from the same veto over EPA rules covering any aspect of energy production, supply, distribution, or use. The public cost is unmitigated pollution from the rules blocked. [S5]

Coal-heavy utilities facing expensive compliance would gain a shield from major rules, but the industry as a whole would face prolonged uncertainty over which rules survive an Energy Department veto. Customers would trade possible bill savings for the health costs of weaker pollution limits. [S2] [S5]
